<explanation>
The project is Wasp – a full‐stack web application specification framework built to “generate” a full React, Node.js (Express), and Prisma app from a concise declarative file (the “.wasp” file). The open‐source repository is the heart of the Wasp universe. Its purpose is to dramatically simplify full-stack web development, making it as rapid as writing just a few lines in a configuration file. It uses a compiler (mostly in Haskell) to translate a high-level declarative specification into boilerplate for the front-end, back-end, and database parts of the application. There are additional packages for deployment, Prisma management, Studio, and tooling, as well as a website with documentation and examples.

To create the best and most accurate system design diagram for Wasp, consider the following steps:

1. Identify the primary components based on the file structure and README:
 • The core compiler (in the “waspc” directory), which is written in Haskell. This component is central; it parses the .wasp file and produces the generated application.
 • The CLI and code generation layer (organized under folders like “waspc/cli” and “waspc/data/Generator”) which implements file copying, template rendering, and generation of the front-end, back-end, and deployment assets.
 • The supporting packages (in “waspc/packages”) for deployment (deploy), Prisma (for database code), Studio (for UI of data), and TypeScript inspection.
 • The examples folder (found also as “examples/…” in the repository) demonstrates concrete full-stack applications built with Wasp.
 • The web folder which is the website with documentation, blog posts, and landing pages; though it is not part of the application runtime, it represents documentation and developer marketing.
 • Ancillary tools (in “waspc/tools”) to help install or package code.

2. Determine relationships and data flows:
 • The Wasp developer writes a “main.wasp” configuration file that describes the app’s high-level aspects, such as app metadata, routes, pages, queries, and even Prisma models.
 • The compiler (waspc) reads this high‐level specification, then uses the generators to produce a full boilerplate application. This includes:
  – A client (React with react-query, etc.) for the front-end.
  – A server (Node.js/Express) for back-end logic including RPC calls and authentication.
  – A Prisma schema for database management.
 • Deployment packages also exist so that the generated code can be deployed on various platforms without lock-in.
 • In addition, the system supports generating configuration for jobs, email sending, and integration with third party auth providers (handled by configurable modules).

3. Diagram Structure Guidelines:
 a. Clearly label each major component:
  – “Wasp Compiler” (the Haskell-based translator).
  – “Specification Input (.wasp file)”
  – “Generators” (dividing into Client Generator, Server Generator, Deployment Generator, etc.)
  – “Generated Web App” that further splits into “Client (React)” and “Server (Express/Node + Prisma)”
  – “Supporting Packages” (Deployment, Prisma, Studio, TS-Inspect, etc.)
  – “Documentation & Website” (separate web folder).
 b. Draw directional arrows to show:
  – The flow of data; for example, from the developer’s specification file into the compiler.
  – The output of various generators into the source directories for the client and server apps.
  – Integration with database via the Prisma models.
 c. Use color coding and shapes so that:
  – Core engine components (the compiler, generator modules) are one color.
  – Application output (Client, Server, Database) are another color.
  – Supporting documentation or external integrations (deployment providers, authentication services) are distinguished by different shapes or colors.
 d. Optionally add notes on versions; for instance, indicate that the current stack supports React + Express + Prisma and highlight the experimental AI code generator (“Wasp AI / Mage”) for starting new projects.

4. Tailor your diagram with design patterns and dependencies in mind:
 • Emphasize the abstraction layers: a simple declarative specification drives massive generated code.
 • Make sure the diagram reflects both the “input” side (specification and high-level design) and the “output” side (the generated, deployable full-stack app).
 • Highlight that the system is “smart” (that is, it uses code generation and abstraction to reduce boilerplate), so you might use a callout or annotation to describe the compiler’s role in bridging high-level design with detailed implementation.
 • Describe that the core engine is highly modular – for example, the “Wasp/AI” modules use OpenAI in some scenarios to generate project boilerplate.

5. Incorporate technologies and sustainability details:
 • Mention that the front-end is built using React (with potential additional libraries like react-query) and uses TailwindCSS (evident from several tailwind.config files).
 • The back-end is built with Node.js (Express is likely used given the “server” folder and common web practices).
 • The Prisma ORM (support files like “schema.prisma”) facilitates database interactions.
 • Deployment is abstract and can be done with different providers using configuration files present in “packages/deploy”.
 • The repository uses modern Haskell tooling (cabal), TypeScript’s tooling (tsconfig.json), and various GitHub workflows for CI.

6. Practical Instructions for the Principal Software Engineer:
 • Begin by sketching a high-level block diagram using your tool of choice (e.g., draw.io, Lucidchart, or even a whiteboard).
 • Begin with a block labeled “Developer Specification (.wasp file)” that feeds into “Wasp Compiler” (Haskell core). Draw an arrow from specification to compiler.
 • From the “Wasp Compiler”, split arrows going into separate generator components:
  – “Client Generator” producing a React-based front-end structure.
  – “Server Generator” producing a Node.js application (which in turn uses Express, Prisma, etc.).
  – “Deployment Generator” which outputs files for containerization or cloud platform deployments.
 • Show that the output components (Client, Server, Database models) integrate together to form the “Generated Web Application.”
 • Include a separate block (or set of blocks) for “Supporting Tools & Packages” that include Deploy (fly, etc.), Prisma tools, Studio, TS-inspect, and others.
 • Optionally add a feedback loop (or annotation) where tests and CI (GitHub workflows) continuously check and validate the generated application.
 • Finally, mention external integrations such as third-party authentication providers (for email, GitHub, Google, etc.) – these can be drawn as external service icons connected with the “Auth” components configured by the user in the .wasp file.
 • Clearly label the technologies used at each part of the system – “React”, “Node.js/Express”, “Prisma”, “Haskell” for the compiler, etc.

In summary, the system design diagram must reflect the following:
 – A declarative input (main.wasp and related config) that is processed by a modular Haskell compiler (Wasp Compiler).
 – Multiple generator modules that output a full-stack app (client, server, and database).
 – Supporting packages and tools that extend functionality (deployment, TS inspection, etc.).
 – A feedback/control loop with testing and CI/CD.
 – The diagram should use clear labels, directional arrows to indicate data flow and dependencies, and color/shape variations to distinguish between core engine components, generated output, external integrations, and documentation/web resources.

By following these detailed guidelines and tailoring your diagram to show the separation between high-level declarative inputs, the compilation process, and the generated full-stack app, you will provide a highly accurate, detailed, and useful architectural overview of the Wasp project.
</explanation>
